abstract.p: Drug-checking services (DCS) provide people who use drugs (PWUD) with crucial information concerning the substances they may consume. The intent of DCS is to reduce harms potentially associated with those substances, by providing evidence-based information about the contents of said substances and possibly influencing PWUD consumption-related behaviors. This pilot project reports on a network of 10 dedicated Raman spectroscopy drug-checking devices, located at various organizations throughout the province of Ontario, Canada. The spectrometers were specifically developed for drug-checking analysis and use machine learning (ML) enabled software to provide participants with automated, real-time results. The same software was also used to collect participants’ demographic data and self-reported consumption-related behavior changes. In this work, we report on the results provided by this network over a 14-months period from July 2023 to August 2024 on 7752 samples provided by 5083 participants. On select samples, high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (HPLC–MS) measurements were also collected to probe the accuracy of the results and quantify variations between the two techniques. Voluntary feedback was also collected from a limited number of participants concerning the potential impact the drug-checking process may have on their consumption-related behaviors.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The narcotic drug crisis in Canada has reached an alarming status due to the widespread use of synthetic opioids such as fentanyl that can contribute to devastating and often times lethal overdoses [1]. Between January 2016 and this past March 2025, there were a total of 53,821 apparent opioid toxicity deaths. 1377 of those, were reported between Jan to March of this year, 2025 [2]. This rapidly rising overdose mortality rate continues to highlight the urgency of developing more efficient and effective means of prevention and response, with one are of focus being drug-checking technologies and their utilization within a larger harm reduction framework. Providing people who use drugs (PWUD) with the opportunity to anonymously have their substances analyzed and quantified can help facilitate timely and targeted public health interventions in secured and equipped spaces such as supervised consumption sites or paramedical mobile units [3, 4].

DCS can be provided on-site using portable devices and off-site using laboratory-based instruments, each with its own respective advantages and limitations [5]. On-site drug-checking provides participants with real-time (within 5 to 15 min) critical information about major active substances and filling agents in their samples, allowing participants to make more informed decisions about their potential consumption-related behaviors prior to, during, or after consumption [6, 7]. Delays in providing information to PWUD concerning the content of their substances may limit the efficacy of drug checking services and may contribute to increased risks associated with their consumption. Additionally, publicly accessible on-site drug-checking gives harm reduction organizations and workers additional opportunities to communicate with PWUD, offering further support and education on safer consumption practices. However, a major limitation of on-site rapid drug-checking technologies is their reduced ability to accurately quantify individual components in a multicomponent sample [8]. Conversely, off-site drug-checking performed in specialized laboratories results in more complete qualitative and quantitative analyses but does not offer the real-time capability and accessibility that on-site facilities provide [9]. This in turn loses the momentum generated from initial sample submission to induce possible changes in participant consumption-related decisions. In addition, logistical issues such as sample transportation and longer analysis times (typically at least a week) can hinder effectiveness, particularly in preventing immediate harms [10]. Balancing the benefits and limitations of both approaches is therefore crucial in implementing comprehensive DCS. Various analytical approaches such as gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC–MS) [11], ion mobility-mass spectrometry (IM-MS) [12], liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC–MS) [13, 14], paper spray-mass spectrometry (PS-MS) [15], nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) [16], capillary electrophoresis [17], and immunoassays [18] have been developed and validated for analysis of drugs. Although the aforementioned techniques are commonly used, high-performance liquid chromatography-mass Spectrometry (HPLC–MS) is widely regarded as “the current gold standard for drug analysis” [19]. Access to large spectral databases of HPLC–MS techniques further facilitates the identification of a myriad of molecules present in samples that can be quantified with proper calibration protocols. Despite the exceptionally high molecular specificity and sensitivity of these techniques, they are sizeable instruments with high maintenance costs that require time consuming protocols and calibrations. These protocols and calibrations are part of the operational expertise costs (i.e. the operator must possess advanced technical expertise to ensure proper operation, maintenance and analysis of the collected results) only further adding to the net costs associated with their use. Further, these instruments need to be operated in designated spaces with specific gas inlet and outlet connections [20, 21]. Due to these limitations, the instruments are generally used off-site and operated in clinical and regulatory analytical laboratories for the detailed analysis of illicit drugs with delayed times associated with the quantity of samples to be analyzed. Alternatively, vibrational spectroscopy techniques such as Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) [22], and Raman spectroscopy [23] are attractive solutions since they are non-destructive, rapid, and can be conducted with smaller, more portable equipment. Non-destructive analysis allows for the sample to be returned to the participant, which could potentially aid in increasing the use of these technologies by people with limited financial means. Optical spectroscopy involves simple preparation for powdered samples, and the devices are notably portable. This allows for easy relocation from site to site or integration onboard a vehicle with no major challenges. Some of these instruments are battery operated and therefore entirely portable, however, they possess a limited library of common compounds [24–26]. In the context of drug-checking technologies with rapid turnaround times, Raman spectroscopy offers notable advantages. These include short acquisition times and high spatial resolution which, when combined with mapping capabilities, can help unravel the complex multicomponent nature of street substances [27]. The primary disadvantage of Raman spectroscopy lies in its reduced performance when samples exhibit fluorescence. Other disadvantages include the lack of reference narcotic libraries at select excitation wavelengths and the difficulty in quantifying potent drug components in a sample, with an extremely high level of accuracy [8, 28].

In this project, a series of 10 identical Raman spectrometers (Scatr Series One, Scatr Inc. Ontario, Canada) were specifically developed for the analysis of street drug at various healthcare organizations across Ontario, where PWUD were provided the opportunity to anonymously test their substances at no cost. The spectrometers are networked, and the collected spectra are uploaded to the cloud and analyzed in real-time using machine learning (ML) models.

This paper reports the findings obtained from this pilot project conducted over 14 months during which 7752 street substances were analyzed from 10 drug-checking sites across Ontario. The objective of this project is to present a snapshot of the distribution pattern and use of illicit drugs in Ontario. All substances were analyzed by the Raman spectrometers and 12.7% (1083) of the samples were voluntarily donated by participants to be further analyzed via HPLC–MS to compare the results. Intake questions and consent were recorded as described in the corresponding Letter of Information and Consent (Supplementary Material-Letter of Information of Consent).

sec.title: Chemicals and standards
sec.p: All chemicals utilized, including solvents and reference standards, were of analytical quality and were used as received without additional purification. The reference control substances including substances explicitly listed in the controlled drugs and substances act (CDSA) used for generating the custom Raman library were purchased from Toronto Research Chemicals under Office of Controlled Substances Exemption 56. The fillers and diluents were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. The reference standards used for the HPLC–MS calibration curves were bought from Sigma Aldrich and the calibrants were prepared by diluting the stock solution in LC–MS grade water. HPLC–MS grade water was obtained from Fisher Scientific and acetonitrile; formic acid and methanol used in HPLC–MS analyses were purchased from Sigma Aldrich.

sec.title: HPLC–MS measurements
sec.p:
The reverse-phase HPLC–MS data were acquired on Agilent 6224 TOF LC/MS equipped with G1329B autosampler, G1312A binary pump and Agilent Infinity Lab Poroshell 120 EC-C18, 3.0 × 50 mm, 2.7 μm column. The column temperature was set to be 30 °C and 5 µL of analyte was infused with a flow rate of 0.75 mL min−1 under gradient elution with water and 0.1% (V/V) formic acid as the aqueous phase and acetonitrile as the organic phase. The elution started from 5% of acetonitrile and gradually increased to 35% over a span of 16 min and was followed by 3 min of system reconditioning phase (Table 1). The mass spectrometer was operated under gentle conditions and in positive polarity using a capillary voltage of 3.5 kV, with a desolvation gas temperature of 325 °C.Table 1

sec.title: Raman measurements
sec.p: The Raman spectrometers (Scatr Series One) incorporate a scanning sample stage to enable surface and depth scanning to collect numerous spectra over the sample, revealing the heterogeneous nature of each sample. Single-point Raman mapping was employed to scan a sample in a systematic grid, collecting individual spectra at discrete spatial locations to construct a chemical distribution map.

The scans are conducted through three selectable scanning modes—Quick (3 min 7 × 7 spectra), Standard (7 min 13 × 13 spectra), and Detailed (13 min 18 × 18 spectra)—which gave participants flexibility to balance analytical resolution with time constraints. Each mode yields a distinct mapping density of the powder sample surface. Excitation wavelength was set to l = 1064 nm to minimize the fluorescence background [29]. The instrument was coupled to a 20 × , 0.4 N.A. microscope objective yielding a spatial resolution of ~ l/(2 NA) = 1.33 µm and a spot size of roughly 2.5 µm. Most scans analyzed in this work were conducted in the standard mode, generating 169 spectra that were then individually analyzed by ML algorithms. Such large datasets maximize the detection of an isolated grain of a given component present in the mixture, thus increasing the probability of detecting substances present in low concentrations or localized regions. As opposed to single point spectroscopy measurements such as in ATR-FTIR (Attenuated Total Reflectance-Fourier Transform Infrared spectroscopy), where the isolated grain would be averaged in the resulting spectrum, the multipoint map reveals the heterogeneity of drug speckles embedded in a filler matrix. The larger the density of collected spectra, the higher the possibility to single out a given aggregate of a drug component.

A dedicated reference database (Supplementary Material-Reference Library) was created for the most common drug samples and fillers currently circulating in Canada. The reference library was continuously updated throughout the project as new psychoactive substances or fillers were detected by other means.

The collected spectra are uploaded in real-time to the cloud and analyzed by ML models. The reference spectra were used by the ML model to determine the contribution of each individual component. All networked spectrometers operated through a web-based dashboard specifically designed for use by site staff with minimal or no scientific background. Thus, data were collected from sites in real-time and centralized by the project team, enabling geographic monitoring of street drug trends across participating locations.

Results are downloaded back to the instrument in real-time, providing immediate feedback from the first collected spectrum. The results are averaged until the last spectra is collected. All spectra are stored in a secured server (Amazon Web Services) and are subsequently used to improve ML analysis. During the collection of the spectra, the participants are invited to complete a survey including demographics, expected content of the sample and anticipated consumption-related behavior of the participant. A calibration procedure enables the autofocusing of the laser beam to maximize the signal from the surface sample. This enhances the accuracy, spatial resolution, and reliability of the collected spectral map and enables clear visualization.

sec.title: Machine learning processing
sec.p: The Raman instruments automate spectral processing and classification through cloud-based ML algorithms. Raman preprocessing involves several critical steps to ensure an accurate interpretation of the spectra. This includes spectral smoothing and denoising, baseline correction and normalization. An adaptive smoothness penalized least squares (asPLS) was used for baseline correction and a sinc kernel approach was used for smoothing/denoising. After these steps, the spectra are ready for further analysis and machine learning classification. Proper baseline correction and smoothing are essential to highlight the true Raman peaks, ensuring subsequent identification and semi-quantification of substances through spectral analysis. The associated software used a neural network (NN), a type of ML, to interpret the intricate patterns found in spectral data. This network consists of multiple neural layers that extract features from the input spectra used for the classification. By training on a comprehensive dataset of known substances, the NN learns to recognize the unique spectral signatures of various compounds, allowing it to distinguish between them. The architecture is optimized for real-time processing, ensuring that results are delivered to participants almost immediately. The limit of detection (LOD) and limit of quantification (LOQ) for fentanyl were determined using a 3-component mixture (fentanyl, mannitol, caffeine) made in the laboratory. Importantly, this LOD and LOQ methodology cannot be used universally for any type of mixture since the Raman scattering cross sections of molecules and precursors used for the synthesis of drugs may be different leading to different Raman intensities. However, this methodology is indicative of the performance ability of the ML approach for this particular 3-component mixture.

sec.title: Sample preparation
sec.p: For HPLC–MS experiments, samples collected from the sites were ground to be homogenized. Subsequently, 3 to 7 mg of the samples were dissolved in 5 ml of a mixture of methanol: acetonitrile: water (2.5: 1.5: 1) followed by sonicating for 10 min to ensure complete dissolution. Afterwards, the solution was filtered through a 0.2 µm filter to remove any insoluble impurities that could potentially interfere with the chromatographic separation or damage the instrument. The obtained solution was then diluted 50-fold with water and injected into the HPLC–MS system. The collected data was acquired using Agilent MassHunter Workstation and was processed using TOF qualitative and quantitative data analysis software (Agilent Technologies, Inc., Santa Clara CA).

For Raman spectroscopy experiments, analysis was performed at each site on powders provided by participants without requiring any extensive sample preparation. The sample was placed on a sample holder in which a (6 × 6 × 2) mm3 cavity was filled with the substance to be scanned. Point-scanning was enabled by an XY sample stage.

Each sample was assigned a unique identification code to ensure accurate traceability while maintaining confidentiality. Participant expectations regarding the contents of their samples were acquired via verbal questioning by the device operator and documented electronically as part of the intake. sec.title: Quantitative performance validation
sec.p:
The quantitative results from the Raman measurements were compared against HPLC–MS as a reference standard. As highlighted in Fig. 3, the Raman results demonstrate a high degree of accuracy, with an error range of 0 to ± 10 percent for 77.8% of fentanyl, 73.3% of methamphetamine, 60.00% of MDMA, 89.3% of xylazine, and 100.00% for benzodiazepine samples. Therefore, the Raman spectra obtained from mapping experiments on street samples and subsequently classified by ML appear to provide reliable results that are close to quantitative HPLC–MS measurements. A noticeable discrepancy is observed for the cocaine-containing samples. Only 35.3% of cocaine-positive samples demonstrated less than ± 10% error range and in 72.6% of the cases, cocaine was over quantified.Fig. 3
Percentage difference between Raman quantification and HPLC–MS as the confirmatory testing method for a positive sample of the substances of interest. A 0% quantification difference indicates a perfect match between both methods, while positive and negative values indicate false positives or false negatives, respectively

sec.title: Raman spectra
sec.p:
Raman spectra for the most common substances are reported in Fig. 4. As can be observed, each compound possesses a distinct vibrational fingerprint arising from its molecular structure that is used as the basis for molecular identification [30]. Nonetheless, in Fig. 5, the Raman spectra of cocaine and benzoylecgonine (the main metabolite of cocaine) [31], have overlapped vibrational modes due to common structural characteristics. Initially, the ML model overestimated the concentration of cocaine in some samples due to the presence of benzoylecgonine. Because benzoylecgonine was not yet included in the spectral database, the model misclassified it as cocaine, leading to inflated quantification results. After benzoylecgonine was added to the database, the reported concentrations of cocaine aligned more closely with the values obtained through HPLC–MS analysis. This scenario illustrates both a limitation and an advantage of the ML classification: when a structurally similar compound is absent from the database, the model may attribute its signature to the closest available analog. However, this limitation can readily be addressed by regular updates to the Raman spectral library. Incorporating new substances, analogs, and precursors as they emerge would ensure the model remains robust and reflective of the evolving unregulated drug supply.Fig. 4
Raman spectra of the pure substances of interest alongside their corresponding chemical structures collected by the Raman instruments. The above spectra are presented after undergoing baseline correctionFig. 5
Raman spectra of cocaine and benzoylecgonine. The structural similarity leads to overlapping spectral features, which can result in misclassification if a ML model is trained on only one compound

sec.title: Frequency of detected opioids and fillers
sec.p:
Figure 6a illustrates the frequency of commonly identified drugs in street samples submitted by participants for analysis using the novel Raman spectrometers. Fentanyl was found to be the most abundant opioid with a 52.5% prevalence. The data illustrates that methamphetamine, benzodiazepines (such as bromazolam and temazepam), xylazine, cocaine, and MDMA were commonly used drugs in Ontario during the study period. Surprisingly, methamphetamine and MDMA were found to be pure in 76.64% and 50.52% of the positive cases, respectively. Moreover, caffeine, erythritol and D-Mannitol were found to be the most prevalent fillers found in 31.9%, 18.5%, and 17.6% of the samples, respectively (Fig. 6b).Fig. 6
a The bar graph illustrates the abundance of each detected drug in all analyzed samples. The x axis shows the prevalence of each drug. b The bar graph shows the most common fillers found in the samples

sec.title: Composition trend change in Ontario
sec.p:
The World Health Organization has reported approximately 600,000 deaths yearly due to opioid poisonings [32]. Fentanyl, a highly potent synthetic opioid, has shown a substantial increase in prevalence since 2016. A significant number of fatal overdoses are related to fentanyl and its analogs. In 2023, 82% of all accidental overdose deaths were attributed to fentanyl. Benzodiazepines and xylazine are studied as compounds of interest due to their synergistic respiratory depressant influence on opioids which yield higher overdose risks. Naloxone is less effective in alleviating the effects of these drugs because they act on different receptors than fentanyl, which creates the need for alternative overdose treatments [33]. Understanding the composition of street drugs is therefore essential for the development of efficient and effective approaches to address the current overdose crisis. The dynamic nature of street drug profiling requires constant observation of the market. Figure 7 illustrates the temporal drug prevalence changes from July 2023 to August 2024 in Ontario. As can be seen, fentanyl exhibits a consistently high prevalence in comparison with the other noted active substances. Considering this information, public health organizations can be given the opportunity to allocate resources more efficiently to better promote the health of PWUD.Fig. 7
Percent prevalence of the samples that contained fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, MDMA, xylazine, and benzodiazepines from July 2023 to August 2024 in Ontario

sec.title: Analytical performance of the HPLC–MS method
sec.p:
The developed HPLC–MS method using the optimized gradient elution was capable of effectively separating 30 common opioids and fillers. The clear peak resolution for most target analytes demonstrates the robustness and efficiency of the applied separation method for complex mixture analyses. Table 5 shows the retention time and m/z of all analytes used in this study. Given that the drugs and fillers are small molecules with molecular weights less than 600 Da, the ESI ions predominantly carry a single positive charge generated by gaining one H+ during the electrospray process. Isomers such as morphine and hydromorphone, and butyryl fentanyl and methylfentanyl, which have identical molecular weights and mass-to-charge ratios, were observed to be well separated in the chromatography column using the developed method. The calibration range for most of the compounds ranged from 0.5 to 20 µg ml−1; for compounds detected in trace levels, the range was selected to be 0.2 to 5 µg.ml−1 with the correlation factors R2 = 0.982–0.997.Table 5

sec.title: Comparative analysis case of HPLC–MS and Raman measurements
sec.p:
As an example, an unknown street substance was evaluated using both methods. Figure 8 shows the Raman spectrum of this unknown sample collected from the Sanguen Health Centre (Fig. 8a), together with the reference spectrum of bromazolam (Fig. 8b), xylazine HCl (Fig. 8c), fluoro fentanyl (Fig. 8d), and fentanyl (Fig. 8e). The strong Raman mode near 1000 cm−1 in fentanyl is generally attributed to symmetric ring breathing modes of the phenyl ring, which involve both in-plane C–C stretching and bending vibrations. The peak observed at the 830 cm−1 region of the street sample spectrum is due to ν (N‐C‐C), ρ (CH2), γ (C‐H), δ (C‐C‐C) vibrations of fluoro fentanyl [34]. The adsorption band at around 630 cm−1 corresponds with C-S bond vibrations of xylazine. In the bromazolam spectrum, the distinct peak observed at 1600 cm-1 is attributed to aromatic C = N symmetric stretch of the diazepine ring due to 1,4-diazepine structural backbone [35]. In addition, a C–Br vibration is shown at 570 cm−1.Fig. 8
Raman reference spectra of a street sample, b pure bromazolam, c pure xylazine HCl, d pure fluoro fentanyl, and e pure methylfentanyl and f pure fentanyl

The same sample was analyzed using HPLC–MS. Figure 9 shows the mass spectrum of the sample with the principal components identified and labeled. Caffeine and D-Mannitol, the two most common fillers, comprised 23.1% and 30.7% of the sample, respectively. Fentanyl is present as 1.2% of the mixture, while its analogs, fluoro fentanyl and methylfentanyl, were present at 7.1% and 12.0%, respectively. The spectrum also displayed prominent peaks for xylazine HCl possessing 4.2% and bromazolam at 5.9% of the sample composition. This spectrum underscores the diversity of substances present, posing significant challenges for both detection and public health and safety. Comparison of the Raman data with that of MS illustrated in this example highlights a reliable methodology of the ML model applied to the collected Raman spectra. However, statistical analysis over larger number of spectra is necessary to converge towards a high degree of specificity and sensitivity such as those reported in Fig. 2 and Table 4. Importantly, complex samples with more components or with masking (fluorescent) compounds (drugs or fillers) can be detrimental to such analysis. For such samples, the use of two or more analytical techniques would be beneficial to provide a more precise determination and distribution of the compounds present in the mixture.Fig. 9
Mass spectrum of the street drug collected from the Kitchener harm reduction site. The charge state of all ions assigned in the spectrum is + 1

sec.title: Detection limit of fentanyl: insights from Raman and HPLC–MS analyses
sec.p:
In order to evaluate the sensitivity and accuracy of the Raman measurements and ML protocol, the limit of detection (LOD) and the limit of quantification (LOQ) were evaluated for fentanyl. The Raman ML algorithm was assessed in its ability to detect fentanyl at varying concentrations, ranging from 10% to as low as 0.1%, in solid mixtures. Given the prevalence of caffeine and mannitol as filling agents in illicit drug markets, this study closely mirrored the composition of typical street samples. Six mixtures were made containing 10, 5, 1, 0.75, 0.5, and 0.1 percent by weight of fentanyl. A total mass of 40 mg was maintained per sample. The mass of caffeine was kept the same, while fentanyl and mannitol were varied. The Raman spectra were acquired from the resulting mixtures using quick (147 spectra per map) and standard (507 spectra per map) three-dimensional scan modes. The Mann–Whitney U test was employed in this analysis to compare the Raman intensity of the 1000 cm⁻1 wavenumber for different fentanyl concentrations and the control sample of pure caffeine or mannitol as shown in Fig. 9. By ranking the intensity values, this nonparametric test assessed whether one sample distribution significantly differed from another, making it an ideal choice for comparing the intensity variations across multiple pixels without assuming equal variance or normality. In the quick scans, the algorithm successfully detected fentanyl in the 10, 5, and 1 percent concentrations; however, it failed to detect fentanyl in concentrations below 1%. On the other hand, the standard scan detected fentanyl as low as 0.1%. Two distinct methods were used to assess the limit of detection (LOD) for fentanyl using the Raman instrument: one based on the software’s ML classification algorithm, and the other based on a hardware-driven approach assessing the detector’s ability to consistently identify a characteristic fentanyl Raman peak. Specifically, the presence and average intensity of the 1000 cm⁻1 peak—attributed to the phenyl ring breathing mode in fentanyl—served as a physical indicator of detection. While the algorithm successfully identified fentanyl at concentrations as low as 0.1% in both two- and three-component mixtures during standard scans, this detection was based on a limited number of pixels within each map. At these lower concentrations, the 1000 cm⁻1 peak did not significantly increase across the full spatial map, indicating limited replicability. In contrast, at concentrations of 1% and higher, the 1000 cm⁻1 peak exhibited a consistent and notable increase in average intensity across the entire scan area, supporting its reliability as a true detection threshold (Fig. 10). Therefore, although 0.1% fentanyl was detected by the algorithm, it may not be reliably replicated across different samples or settings. This study conservatively reports 1% as the replicable LOD for fentanyl in mixtures containing caffeine and/or mannitol.Fig. 10
The mean intensity of the 1000 cm⁻1 peak, averaged across 507 spectra from each map of three-component mixtures, demonstrating that the maximum peak in fentanyl-containing mixtures (blue dots) was significantly higher than in pure caffeine, pure D-mannitol, or a 50/50 mixture of D-mannitol and caffeine (green dots). ***p < 0.001

sec.title: Impact of awareness and scans at public health sites
sec.p:
The participants were asked to provide feedback about the information provided by the analytical results and decisions around consumption of their substance. From measurements performed on 7752 samples, 3902 participants reported on their decision of how they were responding to the outcome of their result, as summarized in Fig. 11. These findings point to the potential public health impacts of this drug-checking service. Notably, 21.9% (3902) of reporting participants stated they would choose to discard their sample entirely after receiving their results. An additional 16.8% of reporting participants stated a choice to reduce their intended dose—both actions that would likely reduce the risk of overdose or adverse events. It is noted that these are participants reported versus observed results. Therefore, these numbers may be influenced by a variety of biases and confounding factors. Although 47.3% of participants reported that the results did not change their intended use, the fact that nearly 40% of participants reported an intention to change use in a risk-reducing direction highlights the potential influence on safer consumption practices. Only 4.6% reported an intention to increase their dose based on the results. These participants reported consumption-related intentions lend further support to the broader adoption of DCS as a pragmatic and evidence-based harm reduction strategy. The results underscore the effectiveness of educational interventions that aim to provide PWUD, with evidence-based analysis and results to best inform their consumption-related decision making and behavior. A call is also made for national prevention strategies, such as peer training in drug-checking who can further aid in concomitant harm reduction strategies and services.Fig. 11
Illicit drug consumption pattern changes based on the participants' feedback from 3902 respondents

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: By analyzing 7752 street drugs collected from 5120 participants of varying ages and genders across Ontario, this pilot study is the most comprehensive investigation of street drugs conducted in Ontario thus far. This study utilized a dedicated network of Raman spectrometers to provide real-time street drug analysis in Ontario, with the primary objective of enhancing public health and reducing overdose risks. Although these devices are not designed to perform at the level of research laboratory instruments such as HPLC–MS, they offer immediate feedback to the participants which is critical for influencing positive consumption-related changes, as reported by 38% of the participants. The LOD and LOQ were determined for the Raman measurements as well as the deviation of the results with respect to HPLC–MS measurements. Overall, the performance of Raman spectroscopy offers an interesting alternative that can be used in conjunction with research grade instrumentation, thus improving harm reduction strategies and public health interventions. The integrated network connectivity—through a web-based dashboard—and the use of simultaneous ML models to interpret complex Raman spectra, provide key benefits such as real-time updates and continuous improvement in model efficiency. The network also offers the possibility to monitor the geographic mobility of substances between distinct geographic locations.
